demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt

issues.explanation: Relationship status 'Divorced' is implausible for age 21 under the validation rules.

issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: The profile lacks coherence with the trauma type and formulation because the dominant symptoms are generic hyperarousal/danger responses and self-harm, while there are no guilt, responsibility, shame, or perpetration-related appraisals/items that would typically anchor a profile for accidentally causing serious injury to another person. This makes the selected Threat and Memory content feel poorly tied to the identified trauma context.

issues.item: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
issues.explanation: Within the active formulation, Memory is strongly linked with Maladaptive Strategies and moderately bidirectional with Threat. The memory items support vivid, fragmented re-experiencing, but the selected maladaptive strategies do not clearly arise from managing those memories: Avoid Thinking fits, but Avoid People and especially Self-Harm are not well explained by the memory content provided.

issues.item: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
issues.explanation: Rage on Recall is the least coherent memory item for this trauma type in the absence of any corroborating interpersonal blame, anger-focused threat, or appraisals. For accidentally injuring another person, rage can occur, but standing alone alongside missing-memory fragments and sensory reliving, it is hard to integrate clinically compared with guilt, horror, or shame-linked recall.

The profile centers on a moral-injury-type accident in which the patient accidentally caused serious injury to another, but the dominant Memory item is intense rage on recall. Rage can occur, but in this trauma context it is much less coherent than guilt, shame, horror, or distress unless there is some clear target for anger, which is not reflected anywhere else in the profile.

Threat items are nonspecific hyperarousal symptoms (startle, sleep, concentration) that do not clearly connect to the selected Memory content or to a defined ongoing sense of danger. Given the formulation, Threat is mainly linked with Memory, so Threat items should plausibly arise from the memory content. Here the memory profile is fragmented, sensory, and rage-based, while Threat does not reflect a matching fear/danger theme, creating a weakly coherent Memory–Threat pairing.

vignette:
Lien traces the scar on her forearm, a silver line from a stray spark years ago, a minor cost of her trade. For eighteen years, welding had been a source of pride—a skill that was precise, powerful, and honest. That all changed four months ago. The memory never arrives as a complete story, only as a jagged collection of sensory snapshots. There is the high-pitched scream of the angle grinder from the next bay over, the sudden, sickening thud of falling steel, and then a different kind of scream. The rest is a blur, a chaotic space she can’t seem to fill in, no matter how many times her mind forces her to try. She feels like she is only remembering parts of what happened, with the crucial moments just before the accident remaining a frustrating blank. What does return, with nauseating clarity, is the taste that filled her mouth in that instant: a coppery, metallic tang of pure panic that she can still taste now, whenever a memory fragment breaks through during the day.

In the weeks that followed the accident that crushed her colleague’s hand, Lien returned to work, believing the familiar routine would be a comfort. It became a minefield instead. The hiss of an acetylene torch or the sudden flare of an arc welder would send a jolt through her body, her heart hammering against her ribs and her palms instantly slick with sweat. Holding her own torch steady felt impossible; her focus would shatter, her mind drifting to the image of twisted metal and the sound of that scream. She was certain that another disaster was imminent, that her carelessness was a fixed part of her character, waiting for another chance to cause harm. This fear made it impossible to concentrate, turning the simplest bead weld into a monumental and terrifying task.

The workshop, once a place of camaraderie, now felt hostile. Lien started eating lunch in her truck, unable to bear the small talk in the breakroom. She imagined her colleagues’ pity and their blame, though no one ever said a word. The avoidance bled into her life outside the shop. She stopped answering calls from her sister, the silence on her end of the line feeling safer than trying to explain the unexplainable weight she carried. When the memories ambushed her, the guilt was a physical force, pressing down on her chest until it was hard to breathe. To keep the thoughts at bay, she would turn the radio up in her truck until the speakers distorted, or work on projects in her garage until she was too physically exhausted to think. But it was a losing battle. The intrusive thoughts were relentless, a constant, looping track of self-recrimination. *I should have double-checked the rig. I was distracted. It’s my fault he can’t support his family.* She would dwell on every tiny decision she made that day, dissecting her actions, always arriving at the same verdict: she was unforgivably negligent.

Sleep offered no escape. She would lie in the dark for hours, her body rigid, her mind replaying the fragments of the accident. When she did finally drift off, she would often wake up abruptly, her heart racing, the metallic taste of fear fresh in her mouth. The exhaustion settled deep into her bones, making her days even more difficult. The final impetus for seeking help came last week, when her supervisor, a man who had mentored her for over a decade, called her into his office. He didn’t mention the accident, but spoke with gentle concern about her declining performance, the missed deadlines, and a near-miss with a piece of equipment that another welder had reported. The shame was overwhelming. Lien is now terrified of losing her job, but more than that, she is terrified of herself—of the danger she believes she now poses to everyone around her. She has come to therapy not with hope for relief, but with a desperate plea to simply be made safe again.
